A private working library for the final SDLCAI 2026 edits: ten talks, three Q&As and the 2:08 mood film. It contains short and detailed summaries, takeaways, 22 quote candidates, 29 clip candidates and cross-session editorial angles.

The most useful direction for reuse is what happens around generated output: deciding what to build, sharing context, understanding changes, verifying them and learning from what reaches production. The sessions offer different experiences and qualifications, not one proven method.

**Editorial wording.** The four ambiguous phrases are selected for reuse as “a customer”, “prompt-survey”, “humans” and “you’re”. The survey term and human/agent comparison are contextual corrections; these candidates are labelled as lightly edited wording. Recognition alternatives remain in the review record. Twenty-one attributions are supported by metadata or context; use the final Q&A session label without an individual speaker name for its quote. Direct listening is not claimed, and clip boundaries remain candidates for review.

**Using the timecodes.** Times refer to the final edited videos, including their title cards. Local review links select a video; seek to the stated time manually. They work on this computer while the [review server](http://127.0.0.1:8766/) is running. Public YouTube video URLs can be added after upload.
# Cross session findings

Across the seminar, faster generation repeatedly exposes work elsewhere in the system: deciding what to build, supplying context, understanding changes, checking them and operating the result. Mo Khazali frames this as delivery-system design; Ohans Emmanuel connects intent, build, QA and production feedback; Sini Tistelgrén describes the fundamentals between a prototype and accepted production delivery. Jenni Kylmäkoski, Jussi Hacklin and Viljami Kuosmanen offer different adoption experiences, with practical lessons about learning, shared assets, permissions and visible work. Muhammad Waseem makes decision rationale and system understanding central. The research sessions broaden this beyond code: Tapio Pitkäranta uses tangible probes for discovery, Joongi Shin studies the experience of people generating interfaces, and Zak Allal describes infrastructure for repeating scientific experiments. These are related perspectives rather than one demonstrated method. The Q&As preserve useful qualifications: building can change the problem being explored; documentation can become a burden; more output can overwhelm expert review; and activity metrics alone do not establish value. A strong editorial direction is therefore to ask what happens around generated output, supported by named examples and the limits of each example.
## Generation changes the delivery system

Mo, Ohans and Sini place generation inside a wider delivery flow. Viljami describes the review and testing work created by more proposals, while the research Q&A describes a similar evaluation constraint in peer review.

# Differences worth preserving
## Separate discovery or learn through building

Tapio’s distinction helps ask whether a team is exploring the right problem or engineering a solution. Joongi’s Q&A response cautions against making that boundary rigid: testing a built artefact can change the problem. Both perspectives should remain visible.

[Tapio Pitkäranta 02:18–04:51](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#tapio-talk) · [Tapio Pitkäranta 12:34–14:35](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#tapio-talk) · [Research Q&A 13:56–16:23](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#research-panel)
## Approval models depend on the work and risk

Viljami retains engineer review and merge for contributions. Sini discusses preapproved routine work and approval based on evidence, with independent verification. Ohans moves consequential review into implementation planning. These are different operating models, not proof of one universal review policy.

[Viljami Kuosmanen 17:37–19:38](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#viljami-talk) · [Sini Tistelgrén 21:47–23:14](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#sini-talk) · [Ohans Emmanuel 09:02–13:04](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#ohans-talk)
## More context also creates maintenance work

Several talks call for explicit knowledge and rationale. The final Q&A raises the cost of accumulating decision files for people and agents. The discussion does not supply a complete policy for pruning and maintaining them.

[Muhammad Waseem 14:59–16:58](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#waseem-talk) · [Viljami Kuosmanen 04:00–05:20](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#viljami-talk) · [Final Q&A 24:29–26:00](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#final-panel)
## Cost visibility and outcome measurement answer different questions

Jussi’s quotas and the industry panel’s subscription and infrastructure discussion concern access and expenditure. Mo’s critique of activity metrics concerns whether the delivery system improves. Tracking token costs and rejecting token volume as proof of value are compatible positions.

# Reuse plan

**2026 archive and video cards.** Use each short summary as a starting point for a video card and each long summary for an archive entry. Preserve the official title, speaker and materials link. Add actual YouTube video URLs after upload; current review links are local.

**Opening editorial article.** How faster generation changes the work around the code: context, verification, operations and choosing what to build. Develop the argument with named speaker examples and keep it framed as seminar synthesis.

**Newsletter series.** Three follow-ups: learning and adoption; decision rationale and review; probes, generative UI and scientific experiments. Select one main example and one useful qualification per issue.

**Clips and discussion prompts.** Start with the bottleneck message, the deployment near miss, the discovery qualification and the documentation burden. Longer Q&A ranges retain the question and caveats. Watch and listen to the selected ranges, confirm wording and panel attribution, and tighten boundaries before rendering.

**Channel introduction.** Use the existing 2:08 mood film as a candidate channel introduction or archive opener. Approve the final film and preserve the required music and photograph credits when making derivatives.

**Discussion prompts**

- Which constraint moved after generation became faster in your team, and what evidence shows it?
- Who owns the reasons behind architectural decisions, and who keeps them useful?
- Which changes can an agent propose, verify, approve, merge or deploy in your system?
- What have you learned about the problem only after building and testing a prototype?
- Which activity metric are you tempted to treat as an outcome, and what denominator is missing?

## Mo Khazali
**1978: The Last Good Year** · 35:50 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#mo-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#mo-khazali-industry-perspective)

**Short summary**

Mo Khazali uses automotive and factory-history analogies to argue that AI adoption needs a redesigned delivery system. Shared platforms, daily learning, early quality checks and customer-outcome measures matter more than token consumption or code output alone.

**Detailed summary**

Mo Khazali compares today's AI adoption with manufacturers investing in automation while leaving their working systems largely unchanged. Through the Detroit, NUMMI and factory-electrification stories, he argues for redesigning the flow of work rather than expecting better tools to repair an organisation by themselves. He applies ideas from the Toyota production system and the Lean Tech Manifesto to software: an AI platform team shares useful building blocks, teams practise daily problem-solving, reference blueprints and deterministic checks catch recurring defects, and the working week is adapted to the team's actual constraints. His examples emphasise learning from friction and feeding local improvements back into the wider organisation. He closes by shifting attention toward what to build and how to measure it: delivery flow, failures, recovery, rework and value for customers, rather than licences, token leaderboards or generated code volume.

**Takeaways**

- 06:43–12:34: Tool adoption and activity measures do not by themselves demonstrate customer value or an improved delivery system.
- 16:44–19:14: An AI platform team can turn local solutions into shared model access, observability, skills, standards and support.
- 19:15–25:43: Daily experiments and root-cause discussions develop a learning culture beyond a one-off rollout or workshop.
- 25:43–28:51: Reference blueprints and deterministic rules can prevent known classes of mistakes and reduce repeated correction.
- 31:43–35:39: Audit the whole flow and track outcomes, failures, rework and customer value as bottlenecks shift toward deciding what to build.

## Ohans Emmanuel

**Zero-trust harnesses for agentic software delivery** · 32:09 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#ohans-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#ohans-emmanuel-industry-perspective)

**Short summary**

Ohans Emmanuel describes a connected delivery workflow that treats agent output as something to verify. Shared intent, early plan review, paired models, visual system understanding, independent QA and production feedback form a loop from deciding what to build through learning from what ships.

**Detailed summary**

Ohans Emmanuel presents the practices his team uses to produce software with coding agents while retaining engineering judgement. A plan or statement of intent must remain accessible to the whole team and to later stages of delivery. Reviewing implementation decisions early can catch a wrong premise before it generates a large diff. His team pairs different models during implementation, focusing escalation on consequential issues rather than endless nitpicks. Visual representations of changes help engineers retain a mental model of architecture and data flow. Independent QA agents exercise preview deployments, combining adaptive interaction with deterministic assertions, and exploratory checks look beyond predefined paths. After deployment, monitoring signals are connected across services and agent traces. Findings feed back into tasks and implementation plans, so the value lies in the connected feedback loop as well as in the individual checks.

**Takeaways**

- 07:03–09:01: Keep shared intent accessible throughout delivery so implementation, QA and operations can refer to the same goal.
- 09:02–13:04: Review implementation decisions early and use model pairing during the build to catch consequential errors before a large diff accumulates.
- 14:49–17:58: Retain a human understanding of system architecture and data flow even when agents produce most changes.
- 17:58–24:59: Separate the implementing agent from QA and combine adaptive checks with deterministic assertions and exploratory testing.
- 24:59–31:58: Connect production signals and feed root-cause learning into the next task, plan and review.

**Quote candidates**

- **15:13–15:20 · Ohans Emmanuel:** “I don't want a world where I don't understand the system that I maintain.”
  The caption candidate is present in both fresh Whisper and independent-family Parakeet ASR after case and punctuation normalization. Editorial listening and approval remain pending.

**Clip candidates**

- **09:02–10:37 · Review the implementation decision before it becomes a large diff** (95s). A concrete design-choice example explains the case for earlier plan review. Audience: Engineers and reviewers working with coding agents.
- **19:30–22:13 · What independent QA needs beyond another model's approval** (163s). Connects shared intent, deterministic assertions, user-level checks and evidence from a separate QA agent. Audience: QA and platform teams.

**Further uses**

- An end-to-end checklist for agent-assisted delivery
- A cross-talk article on retaining system understanding while shipping faster

**Editorial notes**

- The workflow describes the speaker's team experience, not a universal benchmark result.
- The argument for reviewing plans does not mean the workflow dispenses with later QA or human evaluation of the change.
- Model pairing and a separate QA agent are techniques for additional scrutiny, not proof that their failure modes are statistically independent.
- Read-only infrastructure access still carries data-disclosure risks; do not reuse the monitoring discussion as a claim that read-only access is harmless.
## Jenni Kylmäkoski

**Why Leaders Should Use AI Themselves and Eat Their Own Dog Food?** · 25:30 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#jenni-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#jenni-kylmakoski-industry-perspective)

**Short summary**

Jenni Kylmäkoski explains why leaders should build and use AI tools themselves. Her reporting tools and an unintended Jira change reveal practical lessons about onboarding, permissions, observability, learning time and maintaining shared AI assets as products.

**Detailed summary**

Drawing on her work as an R&D leader at Nokia, Jenni Kylmäkoski argues that leaders need direct experience of the changes they ask teams to make. She builds small applications for recurring reporting and analysis, using the same tools as her developers and checking the generated results. This exposes installation friction, documentation gaps and the support people need to adopt new capabilities. A model change unexpectedly reopened closed Jira tickets during a reporting task, prompting her to reconsider permissions, logs and recovery. She also describes the tension between delivery commitments and time spent learning. Her conclusion is that an organisation's prompts, skills, agents, workflows and monitoring need requirements, testing, distribution, documentation and ongoing maintenance, just as other software products do. Practical participation helps leaders understand both the technology and the people living through the transition.

**Takeaways**

- 05:41–09:07: Leaders can learn the development experience by building tools for their own recurring work and validating the outputs.
- 09:07–11:34: Onboarding, documentation, training and support shape whether shared AI assets are actually used.
- 16:00–19:09: A model change can alter tool behaviour; least privilege, logging and recovery deserve explicit attention.
- 19:20–20:50: Learning time must be included in priorities and delivery plans, or urgent commitments will displace it.
- 20:50–22:57: Shared AI assets need a product lifecycle with requirements, tests, releases, documentation and maintenance.

## Tapio Pitkäranta

**The Agentic Probe: The Instrument of Agentic Discovery & Engineering** · 22:39 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#tapio-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#agentic-discovery)

**Short summary**

Tapio Pitkäranta presents agentic probes as tangible experiments that help people clarify problems and explore solutions. Examples from a probe factory and a healthcare process exercise show how faster implementation can move the bottleneck toward ideas, orchestration and validation.

**Detailed summary**

Tapio Pitkäranta separates upstream discovery from downstream engineering while treating their boundary as overlapping rather than fixed. In joint research with Leena Pitkäranta, an agentic probe is a tangible artefact that people can inspect, reject and refine. It might be software, a simulation or another representation of a problem or possible solution. Tapio describes workshops where increasing demand moved the bottleneck from generating ideas to implementing them, leading to a small factory in which agents produced probes from submitted requests. He then outlines work in progress using agentic search to map healthcare processes and imagine alternatives. The point of these examples is to support conversation and validation, rather than to treat generated proposals as deployed solutions. As implementation gets faster, deciding what to investigate and judging whether the result satisfies real constraints become more prominent parts of the work.

**Takeaways**

- 02:18–04:51: Discovery and engineering address different questions, and their boundary can overlap.
- 12:34–14:07: A tangible probe gives people something to react to when their intent is hard to specify in advance.
- 12:34–14:35: Probes can test the understanding of a problem as well as demonstrate a possible solution.
- 15:35–17:48: Scaling implementation shifts constraints toward idea generation, orchestration and human validation.
- 17:50–20:43: Agentic search can inform alternative process designs, but imagined healthcare workflows remain exploratory proposals.

## Joongi Shin
**Generative UI for users, not just for designers** · 19:22 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#joongi-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#joongi-shin-ui-perspective)

**Short summary**

Joongi Shin studies generative UI for people who want to complete a task, rather than design an interface. His comparison of prompts, editable subtask representations and follow-up surveys shows why helping users form and express their intentions matters alongside generating working software.

**Detailed summary**

Joongi Shin asks whether generative UI approaches developed for designers also help everyday, task-oriented users. He explains the challenge of envisioning what an interface should do and articulating that intention to a model. A study with 30 participants compared prompt-only interaction, editable subtask–UI representations and a prompt-survey approach, examining both interface generation and subsequent use. He reports that subtask–UI interaction felt least usable, while prompt-only interaction felt least aligned with users' intentions. Experiences during generation were associated with perceptions of the resulting interface, and participants' prior experience also mattered. Follow-up questions offered useful support for envisioning and articulation, but could become repetitive or miss what users were trying to achieve. His conclusion is to design for the user's actual goal: help people discover what they need without requiring them to become interface designers.

**Takeaways**

- 02:29–05:02: Task-oriented users and designers have different goals and willingness to edit detailed interface specifications.
- 06:52–08:24: Envisioning a useful outcome and expressing it in a prompt are separate sources of difficulty.
- 12:08–13:10: Evaluate the process of generating an interface and the experience of using it, rather than the generated artefact alone.
- 13:10–15:32: In the reported study, subtask–UI interaction felt least usable and prompt-only interaction felt least aligned with intent.
- 16:20–18:40: Follow-up questions can reduce articulation effort, but persistent or irrelevant questioning can also obstruct exploration.

**Quote candidates**

- **15:35–15:42 · Joongi Shin:** “what works for designers may not really work for task-oriented users.”
  Whisper supports the caption wording. Parakeet supports the same content but includes “uh” before “task-oriented users” in both decoders. Treat the candidate as speech with a filler omitted, not a strict verbatim transcript.
- **17:26–17:32 · Joongi Shin:** “the prompt-survey approach can also fail.”
  Lightly edited wording: “prompt-survey” preserves the method named on the slide and in the preceding sentence. ASR renders “problem survey” in this utterance; that alternative remains in the review record. Suggested paraphrase (not verbatim): The prompt-survey approach can fail when follow-up questions do not serve the user’s task.

**Clip candidates**

- **15:32–17:16 · Help people envision without making them design** (104s). Explains the design-versus-use distinction and why prompts or detailed intermediate representations may each leave a gap. Audience: Product designers and teams building AI interfaces.
- **17:16–18:40 · When clarification questions get in the user's way** (84s). Preserves the limitation of survey-based interaction and the value of showing something before every detail is specified. Audience: Builders of assistants and generative UI tools.

**Further uses**

- An article on the cost of asking users too many clarifying questions
- A research summary distinguishing interface generation from task completion

**Editorial notes**

- The findings concern the described study and measured perceptions; they do not establish that one interaction method is universally best.
- The relationship between effort during generation and later usability perceptions is an association, not a demonstrated causal effect.

Jussi Hacklin describes how Elisa supports AI adoption within regulatory and customer-contract constraints. Legal collaboration, clear leadership expectations, practical guidance, shared tooling and bounded experiments form the basis for adoption across the software lifecycle.

**Detailed summary**

Jussi Hacklin describes Elisa's progression from individual AI experiments toward broader use across software development, testing and maintenance. Regulation and customer contracts constrain which tools and data flows are available, so the organisation works with legal specialists and established vendors while separating especially restricted areas from the wider operation. Practical support includes concise guidance, training, a developer portal, a community for sharing experience and central management of tools and quotas. Sandboxed greenfield experiments provide space to try different development approaches. Jussi also sketches a development model connecting product creation, engineering and operations through live, secure organisational context and feedback. He emphasises that adoption depends on people understanding the direction and expectations, alongside a curated tool portfolio that can change as capabilities, pricing and constraints evolve.

- 07:32–09:37: Clear management expectations should be backed by accessible guidance, training and a developer community.
- 09:09–11:27: Central tool ownership and quota monitoring provide visibility while allowing teams to request capacity and propose useful additions.
- 11:28–12:19: Sandboxed experiments can test new development approaches without imposing every brownfield constraint on the experiment.
- 13:59–20:37: Shared context and feedback should connect product creation, development and operations; leadership should keep communicating the direction while adapting the tools.

## Sini Tistelgrén
**AI Factory doesn't eliminate the fundamentals** · 28:10 · [Local review](http://127.0.0.1:8766/#sini-talk) · [Session page](https://www.sdlcai.org/2026/schedule/#ai-factory-fundamentals)

**Short summary**

Sini Tistelgrén describes an AI factory as a delivery system built on intent, architecture, security, independent verification, ownership and operational feedback. She explains why a quick prototype still needs a production path, and proposes bounded loops with executable controls and evidence.

**Detailed summary**

Sini Tistelgrén argues that generating code quickly does not remove the work of taking a change safely into production. Her AI factory connects six stations—intent, design, build, verify, release and operate—through shared foundations and explicitly owned checks. In enterprises, much of the difficulty lies in making existing architecture, data ownership, business rules and decision reasons accessible to agents. She describes assessment findings in which unclear requirements, competing rules, weak testing, ambiguous release ownership and missing production feedback push risk downstream. A delivery-address example illustrates how acceptance criteria, architectural rules, independent verification, controlled release and rollback could work together. Routine changes may use pre-approved policies while people remain responsible for intent, controls and exceptions. She recommends starting with one loosely coupled value stream, measuring its baseline and reinvesting capacity in the surrounding delivery system.

**Takeaways**

- 01:34–03:58: A working prototype expresses intent but still needs the architecture, access, release, operations and support work required for production.
- 06:30–08:04: An AI factory should connect intent, design, build, verification, release and operation through shared fundamentals.
- 09:40–13:49: Agents need written domain rules, tested interfaces, decision reasons and bounded access to the architecture the organisation actually has.
- 21:47–23:14: Control ownership and independent verification matter; the author of a change should not be its sole approver.
- 26:11–27:44: Start with one bounded value stream and a baseline, then measure lead time, failed changes and the cost of accepted delivery rather than output volume alone.

**Short summary**

Zak Allal argues that lowering the cost of repeating experiments can change scientific discovery. He describes a clinical research system built with supercomputing, Rust, Julia and C++, and presents a proposed continuous hearing atlas as an example of questioning the assumptions behind existing categories.

**Detailed summary**

Zak Allal links software architecture and multidisciplinary curiosity to the practical ability to repeat scientific experiments. A weather-checking analogy introduces the cost of time, effort and repetition; he then applies that idea to research tooling and supercomputing. He describes a container-based clinical research system using Rust, Julia and C++ to orchestrate repeatable analyses of hearing data. Repeated experiments produced inconsistent categories, prompting him to question the premise that hearing should be represented as discrete types. He presents a proposed five-dimensional hearing atlas and describes methodological issues he believes affected earlier work, including discretisation and treating paired observations as independent. At the event, he states that the paper is a preprint undergoing review and that regulatory qualification has been sought. The reusable engineering lesson is to make experiments cheap to rerun, preserve their configuration and remain willing to challenge the question being asked.

**Short summary**

Muhammad Waseem argues that AI makes code generation easier while understanding, integration and ownership remain difficult. He examines repository context, decision rationale and agent-facing applications, then proposes deterministic checks, human judgement and gates for safety, architectural fit and measurable value.

**Detailed summary**

Muhammad Waseem organises the talk around writing, reading, deciding and caring for software. Faster generation expands the scope in which mistakes can propagate, while file-level success can conceal broken relationships elsewhere in a repository. His account of a Java refactoring study motivates attention to dependencies and system-level evaluation. He then examines how review capacity, limited agent memory and unwritten organisational knowledge constrain adoption. Decision reasons, rejected options and ownership are not fully represented by source code. Looking ahead to applications whose users include other agents, he discusses intent, contracts and the ability to replace models, tools and agents while retaining control of data and knowledge. His proposed response combines deterministic checks with human evaluation of consequential cases, and asks whether a change is safe, grounded in its environment and producing the intended value.

**Takeaways**

- 07:09–11:01: Measure whether generated changes fit and preserve the system, rather than judging a file or snippet in isolation.
- 11:01–14:58: Review and understanding have to keep pace with generated work; more code alone does not remove that constraint.
- 14:59–16:58: Decision rationale, rejected options, constraints and agreement need to be recorded because code does not contain all organisational knowledge.
- 21:11–22:26: Design for replacement of models, tools and agents while retaining ownership of the data and associated knowledge.

The research Q&A connects agentic probes with the challenge of helping users envision an interface. Tangible examples can support reflection, but their design and information content still matter. The mood film presents SDLCAI as a meeting point for software practitioners and researchers. The official logo leads into event footage, followed by a music-led sequence of talks, discussion, posters and conversations. Two spoken excerpts give the montage a clear editorial thread: Sini Tistelgrén asks whether what is being built is relevant and valuable, and Jenni Kylmäkoski reflects on learning from mistakes. Sponsor thanks and the SDLCAI website close the film. It is suitable as an archive introduction or channel trailer after approval, with the talks and Q&As supplying the fuller arguments behind its short excerpts.

**Takeaways**

- 00:00–01:52: The film connects software practice, research and conversation rather than presenting a single technical conclusion.
- 00:35–01:16: Its two spoken messages concern the value of what is built and the learning that comes from experience.

# Source and review notes

The assistant read all current final captions; reviewed delivery metadata and chapters; drafted summaries, takeaways and synthesis; inspected one sampled frame per clip candidate; and compared every quote against fresh local ASR of audio extracted from the corresponding final review video. A subsequent pass checked six wider context windows with unquantized Whisper large-v3 and reviewed the panel handoffs. This was not direct listening or independent-model-family verification. An independent-family Parakeet-MLX pass then checked all 22 quote windows and six wider context windows, with beam-decoder checks on ten flagged windows. It supports 16 normalized candidate wordings, identifies two speech-edit differences and leaves four exact-wording flags. A focused Parakeet follow-up used 15 predefined clause, sentence and wider-context crops from the final 4K masters, including the original source of the mood excerpt. Both greedy and beam decoders were run on each crop; the noun, article and pronoun variants and one empty result are retained without choosing only a preferred output. For reuse, four ambiguous phrases now have editorial selections that combine the recognition evidence with the named method and surrounding argument. The selected text is labelled as lightly edited wording; the source captions, audio and all recognition alternatives are preserved.

Whisper.cpp large-v3-q5_0 and unquantized large-v3, plus Parakeet-MLX 0.5.3 with mlx-community/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3. All audio processing was local. The Parakeet pass provides a comparison across model families; greedy/beam variants within it are correlated checks.

- No human listening pass or complete motion-video review was performed for this library.
- Four ambiguous phrases have editorial selections: “a customer”, “prompt-survey”, “humans” and “you’re”. The survey term and human/agent comparison are contextual corrections, not verified strict-verbatim transcriptions. Two other candidates omit fillers or restarts. The final-panel respondent remains individually unconfirmed.
- Speaker-reported figures, historical analogies, company outcomes, medical/research claims and vendor anecdotes have not been independently fact-checked.
- Takeaways summarize the speakers’ arguments. Cross-session themes are editorial synthesis, not proof of consensus or effectiveness.
- Mood-film derivative uses must preserve the music and photograph attribution from the delivery package; those licences do not establish rights to all footage.

The four selected readings can be reused as lightly edited wording or paraphrases. Use the final Q&A session label without an individual speaker name for its quotation. Clip boundaries and audiovisual presentation remain separate editorial checks.

The structured companion, `content-library.json`, retains per-video metadata, final-caption fingerprints, quote contexts and ASR comparisons, candidate ranges and cross-session evidence references. `validation-report.json` records the range and source checks. The source videos remain in the local post-production archive.
